x.ASV: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David. Blessed is he that considereth the poor: Jehovah will deliver him in the day of evil.
x.Darby: To the chief Musician. A Psalm of David. Blessed is he that understandeth the poor: Jehovah will deliver him in the day of evil.
x.KJV: To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the Lord will deliver him in time of trouble.
x.YLT: To the Overseer. --A Psalm of David. O the happiness of him Who is acting wisely unto the poor, In a day of evil doth Jehovah deliver him.

nt: David is using the phrase **The happinesses of** to express a strong feeling of admiration. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could express the idea of how fortunate such a person is. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is the one considering]

David is using the adjective **lowly** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are lowly]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **day**, time, or occasion that is characterized by **evil**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When evil things are happening]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [harmful things]

t: and/ he will preserve alive/ him

x.ASV: Jehovah will preserve him, and keep him alive, And he shall be blessed upon the earth; And deliver not thou him unto the will of his enemies.
x.Darby: Jehovah will preserve him, and keep him alive; he shall be made happy in the land; and thou wilt not deliver him to the will of his enemies.
x.KJV: The Lord will preserve him, and keep him alive; and he shall be blessed upon the earth: and thou wilt not deliver him unto the will of his enemies.
x.YLT: Jehovah doth preserve him and revive him, He is happy in the land, And Thou givest him not into the will of his enemies.

nt: The expression **be called happy** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will call him happy]

David switches to addressing Yahweh directly in order to make his conclusion more vivid. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the third person for consistency. Alternate translation: [so may Yahweh not give him]
Here, **soul** represents “desire.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [over to the desire of his enemies]

x.ASV: Jehovah will support him upon the couch of languishing: Thou makest all his bed in his sickness.
x.Darby: Jehovah will sustain him upon the bed of languishing: thou turnest all his bed in his sickness.
x.KJV: The Lord will strengthen him upon the bed of languishing: thou wilt make all his bed in his sickness.
x.YLT: Jehovah supporteth on a couch of sickness, All his bed Thou hast turned in his weakness.

nt: The psalmist is speaking of the person’s time of illness as if it were **the bed of suffering** on which the person lies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his sickbed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **suffering**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when he suffers]

As he did in the previous verse, David switches to addressing Yahweh directly in order to make his conclusion more vivid. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the third person for consistency. Alternate translation: [Yahweh transformed]

By **transformed each bed of his in his sickness**, David means that Yahweh transforms his illness into health. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh transformed his sickness into health]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sickness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when he is ill]

x.ASV: I said, O Jehovah, have mercy upon me: Heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee.
x.Darby: As for me, I said, Jehovah, be gracious unto me: heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee.
x.KJV: I said, Lord, be merciful unto me: heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee.
x.YLT: I--I said, `O Jehovah, favour me, Heal my soul, for I did sin against Thee,'

nt: The pronoun **I** refers to David. David is stating the pronoun **I** separately for emphasis even though the verb translated as **I said** already includes this meaning. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I, David, said]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear as modeled in the UST.

David is using the term **soul** to mean his entire person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Please make me whole again]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since I have sinned against you, I need you to heal me]

x.ASV: Mine enemies speak evil against me, saying, When will he die, and his name perish?
x.Darby: Mine enemies wish me evil: When will he die, and his name perish?
x.KJV: Mine enemies speak evil of me, When shall he die, and his name perish?
x.YLT: Mine enemies say evil of me: When he dieth--his name hath perished!

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in [verse 1](../041/001.md). Alternate translation: [harmful things]

David’s enemies are using the question form to express their hostile wish that David would die. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We wish he would die and his name would perish!]

Here, **his name** represents “his memory” or “his reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the memory of him will perish]

x.ASV: And if he come to see me, he speaketh falsehood; His heart gathereth iniquity to itself: When he goeth abroad, he telleth it.
x.Darby: And if one come to see [me], he speaketh falsehood; his heart gathereth wickedness to itself: he goeth abroad, he telleth [it].
x.KJV: And if he come to see me, he speaketh vanity: his heart gathereth iniquity to itself; when he goeth abroad, he telleth it.
x.YLT: And if he came to see--vanity he speaketh, His heart gathereth iniquity to itself, He goeth out--at the street he speaketh.

nt: Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and intentions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his mind plans evil]

The pronouns **he** and **his** in this verse refer to one of David’s enemies mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And if one of my enemies comes]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **worthlessness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he speaks empty words] or [he pretends to be friendly]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts exist so the phrase **his heart gathers iniquity to itself** means that the enemy is secretly trying to think of bad things to say about David. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he thinks of evil things he can say]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [ways to defame]

x.ASV: All that hate me whisper together against me; Against me do they devise my hurt.
x.Darby: All that hate me whisper together against me; against me do they devise my hurt.
x.KJV: All that hate me whisper together against me: against me do they devise my hurt.
x.YLT: All hating me whisper together against me, Against me they devise evil to me:

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in [41:1](../041/001.md). Alternate translation: [things that will harm me]

x.ASV: An evil disease, say they, cleaveth fast unto him; And now that he lieth he shall rise up no more.
x.Darby: A thing of Belial cleaveth fast unto him; and now that he is laid down, he will rise up no more.
x.KJV: An evil disease, say they, cleaveth fast unto him: and now that he lieth he shall rise up no more.
x.YLT: A thing of Belial is poured out on him, And because he lay down he riseth not again.

nt: David’s enemies are speaking of **A matter of wickedness** as if it were a liquid that is **poured** on a person. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Something wicked has overwhelmed him]

The expression **is poured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Terrible things are happening to him]

This is the beginning of what David’s “haters” (enemies mentioned in the previous verse) are saying about him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of SPEAKER. Alternate translation: [My enemies are saying, “A matter of wickedness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something very evil]

David’s enemies are referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **he who has lain down will not repeat to rise**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will die from this illness]

x.ASV: Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, Who did eat of my bread, Hath lifted up his heel against me.
x.Darby: Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I confided, who did eat of my bread, hath lifted up [his] heel against me.
x.KJV: Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
x.YLT: Even mine ally, in whom I trusted, One eating my bread, made great the heel against me,

nt: David is using **the man of my peace** as a common expression of his culture to mean “my close friend” or “my trusted ally.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my closest ally]

It might seem that the expression **whom I trusted in him** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [in whom I trusted]

David is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food or in general so **the eater of my bread** here means “the one who shared meals with me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who ate meals with me]

David is using **has made great the heel against me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “has greatly betrayed me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has greatly turned against me]

x.ASV: But thou, O Jehovah, have mercy upon me, and raise me up, That I may requite them.
x.Darby: But thou, Jehovah, be gracious unto me, and raise me up, that I may requite them.
x.KJV: But thou, O Lord, be merciful unto me, and raise me up, that I may requite them.
x.YLT: And Thou, Jehovah, favour me, And cause me to rise, And I give recompence to them.

nt: Here, **so that** marks **I may repay them** as the goal or purpose of **be gracious to me and raise me up**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that I may repay them]

x.ASV: By this I know that thou delightest in me, Because mine enemy doth not triumph over me.
x.Darby: By this I know that thou delightest in me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me.
x.KJV: By this I know that thou favourest me, because mine enemy doth not triumph over me.
x.YLT: By this I have known, That Thou hast delighted in me, Because my enemy shouteth not over me.

nt: Here, **shout** represents “triumph.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my enemy does not triumph over me]

x.ASV: And as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, And settest me before thy face for ever.
x.Darby: But as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, and settest me before thy face for ever.
x.KJV: And as for me, thou upholdest me in mine integrity, and settest me before thy face for ever.
x.YLT: As to me, in mine integrity, Thou hast taken hold upon me, And causest me to stand before Thee to the age.

nt: The pronoun **I** refers to David. David places this pronoun at the front of the sentence for emphasis, contrasting himself with his enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But as for me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **integrity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I am honest]

Here, **to your face** represents being in front of or in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

x.ASV: Blessed be Jehovah, the God of Israel, From everlasting and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen.
x.Darby: Blessed be Jehovah, theGod of Israel, from eternity to eternity! Amen, and Amen.
x.KJV: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen.
x.YLT: Blessed is Jehovah, God of Israel, From the age--and unto the age. Amen and Amen.

nt: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let us all praise Yahweh]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

David is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **from the everlasting** and **unto the everlasting**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before time began and continuing forever]
